newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Dec 31.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Dec 31.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
DAILY TELEGRAPH
-- LANG STRIKES OUT FOR FRIENDLY EURO-LABEL

Trade and industry secretary, Ian Lang, is celebrating a victory over Brussels bureaucracy after the trade department persuaded the European Commission to make labelling easier for manufacturers of personal protective equipment. The directive will allow the makers of such products as gardening gloves and protective footwear to drop the date information in the certification marking on their equipment. The benefits from dropping one line could be equivalent to five percent of turnover a year.
-- BILL OF 4.7 BILLION STG FOR PENSIONS ADVICE

A survey by the TUC of attempts to compensate people wrongly advised to buy personal pensions instead of remaining in or joining company schemes, claims that compensation payments for bad advice on personal pensions could total 4.7 billion stg, more than double earlier estimates. Fund managers and regulatory authorities are also criticised. TUC general secretary, John Monks, says that this is the biggest financial scandal ever.
-- CRESTCO BID FOR SUPREMACY REBUFFED BY LIFFE

An attempt by the Bank of England-led electronic settlement system, CrestCo, to turn itself into the supreme authority for regulating the City's back office share dealing is running into trouble. CrestCo wants its own code of fines and disciplinary sanctions against those who fail to settle bargains promptly. Some in the City see the move as an attempt by Crest to deflect back on to dealing firms and registrars some of the blame for the backlog of non-completed transactions.
THE TIMES
-- BARINGS TOPS BID LEAGUE

Barings has topped the league table for takeover and acquisition work, compiled by Acquisitions Monthly magazine, for the second year running. The bank, bankrupted last year by the activities of rogue trader Nick Leeson, advised on a greater value of deals than any of its City rivals. Barings advised on 31 deals worth a total of 11.8 billion stg. Barings was helped by its rescue by ING, the Dutch banking and insurance group.
-- CHAIRMAN OF LLOYD'S HEADS HONOURS LIST FOR BUSINESS

The New Year's Honours List has appointed David Rowland, chairman of Lloyd's of London, a knight for his services to the insurance industry. His knighthood will anger dissident Names, who resent demands for the payment of funds. He joins Bob Horton of Railtrack, Bridget Ogilvie of Wellcome Trust and Ken Trench of Maxwell pensioners' fame. Chairman of the London Metal Exchange, Raj Bagri, is created a life peer.
-- AEGON BUYS US RIVAL FOR 3.5 BILLION DOLLARS

The Dutch parent company of UK insurer Scottish Equitable, Aegon, is expanding in America with the 3.5 billion dollar acquisition of Providian Corporation. The purchase will boost overall earnings per share by five percent in 1998. Aegon has also set aside one billion stg to spend in the UK. Further consolidation in the European market is now likely as insurers face high costs and tough competition from banks and mutual funds.
THE GUARDIAN
-- NEW GLOOM ON BUSINESS FAILURES

According to a report from Dun and Bradstreet, the business information service, Britain's economic recovery may be weaker than previously assumed. The report suggests that the fall in the annual rate of business failures has almost dried up while the number of business failures is still running at 790 a week. The survey reports there were 41,107 business failures in 1996, a drop of 0.5 percent on the figures for the previous year.
-- RAIL FARES CUT TO TAKE ON AIRLINES

A price war has erupted between airlines and rail companies, with rail fares between London and Scotland being slashed. The Great North Eastern Railway, owned by Sea Containers and operator of the East Coast mainline service, cut the price of a single fare from 45 to 19 pounds stg. This has undercut scheduled air fares and brought tariffs closer to coach fares. The move follows GNER's decision to cut fares from Scotland to London to 19 pounds stg.
-- WATER STOPS AT FREE-MARKET LOCK

Ministers are believed to be close to a decision to leave water companies as the only utilities subject to detailed regulation rather than market forces of competition. This will mean abandoning plans to introduce widespread competition into the water industry on the grounds that it wound be costly and impracticable. The move would strengthen the policing role of industry regulator Ian Byatt at a time when his counterparts are relying more on competition to improve efficiency and services.
THE INDEPENDENT
-- SORRELL CLOSE TO 3.6 MILLION STG SHARES BONANZA

Martin Sorrell, chief executive of advertising giant WPP, is near to a multi-million stg pay-out under the incentive scheme established earlier this year. He will be awarded shares worth 3.6 million stg if the WPP share price remains above 230 p until March. The conditions attached to the incentive package, approved by shareholders in the summer, were defended by Sorrell and the WPP remunerations committee as "nearly impossible" to achieve.
-- CHRISTMAS ALL OVER AGAIN AS THE FTSE SMASHES 4,100 BARRIER

The blue chip FTSE 100 index has powered through the 4,100 barrier to a record close putting the stock market at an all-time high. The pound hit a four-year high against the Japanese yen and ended near its peak against the German mark. The index was fuelled by the breaking of new records on Wall Street, where the Dow was showing a reading of 22 points higher as London closed.
-- MANUFACTURING IN UK CONTINUES TO GO DOWNHILL

According to figures from a European labour force survey, only two British areas remain in the "top 20" manufacturing regions in Europe. Based on the percentage of the workforce employed in the sector, only the East Midlands, with 35.4 percent in manufacturing, and the West Midlands, with 34.4 percent, are among the top regions. The top region was Baden-Wuerttemberg in Germany, with 43 percent of employment in manufacturing, and second is Lombardy in Italy, with 42 percent.
